newsitem.title: USA: Conn. lawmakers challenge Gov's choice of tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Conn. lawmakers challenge Gov's choice of tax cuts.

text.p: Democratic leaders of the Connecticut legislature urged property tax relief instead of the cuts in income and gasoline taxes that Republican Governor John Rowland proposed in his fiscal 1998 budget on Thursday.

"I'm very concerned that the governor did not propose cutting the one tax that is the most burdensome to homeowners, renters, and business owners alike -- the property tax," House Speaker Thomas Ritter told a news conference.
Later, a Rowland spokesman said he was encouraged the Democrats shared the governor's desire to cut taxes and spending and added that Rowland was "completely open" to debate over the details.

Democrats, who control both houses of Connecticut's General Assembly, told the news conference that the spending cuts Rowland proposed to finance $430 million in proposed cuts to income and gasoline taxes were too vague. They also charged him with trying to recoup lost revenue through elimination of future cuts in other taxes and hikes in other taxes and fees.
"It is a budget which talks about cutting taxes but unfortunately pays for many of those tax cuts by simply raising other taxes," said Kevin Sullivan, Senate president pro-tempore.
"It's like a shell game -- only this time, there's no pea," said Senate Majority Leader George Jepsen.

But Sullivan said "all of us here clearly agree with the overall message that was presented yesterday. Like the governor, we are committed to cutting spending in the state of Connecticut, and like the governor, we are committed to cutting taxes in the state of Connecticut."

The Democrats also slammed Rowland's proposal to cut state support to Connecticut's public colleges and universities by 10 percent. Connecticut's educators have predicted hundreds of layoffs, the shutdown of entire departments and another possible round of tuition increases if the cuts go through.

Rowland said Thursday his two-year budget represents a 0.4 percent spending cut in the first year, to $10.16 billion, and a 1.4 percent increase in the second year, to $10.31 billion. Sullivan said Rowland's budget message "was really about wrong priorities -- cuts to education, cuts to the environment, cuts to the elderly."
"Connecticut ought to be able to do better than a cheap bridge to nowhere, and unfortunately that is what we have been presented to work with over the next session," Sullivan said.
Ritter contended that many state Republicans had privately voiced their own disappointment in the budget, and that they hoped the Democrats would do the dirty work by insisting on major overhauls.
Dean Pagani, Rowland's press secretary, said after the news conference that he was encouraged by the Democrats' basic agreement with Rowland on the bottom line.

"The important thing that I thought came from the news conference was that the Democrats agreed that the commitment ought to be to holding the line on spending and cutting taxes," Pagani told Reuters.
"If that's the case, then the people of Connecticut have already won."

"Everybody wants to hold the line on spending, and everybody wants to cut taxes. The debate is going to be over how to get there, and which taxes to cut. The governor is completely open to the debate," Pagani said.
